Building a personal Arch Linux

**Operating system:** Arch Linux

**Desktop compositor:** Hyprland

**Display protocol:** Wayland

**Display manager:** Ly

**Terminal emulator:** Kitty

**File manager:** Dolphin

**Status bar:** Waybar

1. Project Goal

My goal is to build a custom Arch Linux system from the ground up while learning how Linux works internally.

Rather than installing a complete desktop environment such as KDE Plasma or GNOME, I want to assemble my own graphical environment from individual components.

I want to understand what each component does, how the components interact, and how to configure the system without depending on blindly copied configurations.

My long-term objectives are to:

  • Understand the Arch Linux installation and boot process.
  • Configure and maintain my own Linux system.
  • Build a customized Wayland desktop using Hyprland.
  • Learn how Linux services, processes, permissions, and configuration files work.
  • Customize window management, transparency, animations, colors, fonts, and application launchers.
  • Manage my desktop configuration through dotfiles and Git.
  • Make the system reproducible so I can restore it after reinstalling Arch or transfer it to another computer.
  • Keep the installation minimal and understand why each package is installed.

I also want to use this project to deepen my knowledge of Linux administration, which is relevant to my longer-term interest in cybersecurity.

# 2. First Arch Linux Installation

2.1. Partitioning and Filesystems

I installed Arch Linux manually on my laptop, replacing Windows 11.

I did not need to preserve the previous operating system or its data.

I used a GPT partition table and created two main partitions:

| Partition | Filesystem | Mount point | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | EFI System Partition | FAT32 | /boot | Stores UEFI bootloader files | | Root partition | ext4 | / | Stores the Linux filesystem and installed system |

The EFI partition was approximately 1 GiB.

I mounted the root filesystem under /mnt and mounted the EFI partition at /mnt/boot before installing the base system.

### What I learned

The EFI System Partition is used by UEFI firmware to locate and execute bootloaders.

The root filesystem contains the Linux operating system, including system files, configuration files, installed applications, and user directories.

The mount point /boot determines where the EFI partition is accessible inside the installed system.

2.2. Installing the Base System

I installed the essential packages:

  • base
  • linux
  • linux-firmware
  • networkmanager
  • sudo
  • nano
  • man-db
  • man-pages

I generated /etc/fstab to define the filesystems that should be mounted during boot.

I then entered the new installation using arch-chroot.

2.3. Initial System Configuration

Inside the installed system, I configured:

  • The timezone for Costa Rica.
  • The system locale.
  • The hostname: archbook.
  • The /etc/hosts file.
  • The root password.
  • A regular user named Jorch.
  • NetworkManager.

I enabled NetworkManager so the network service would start automatically.

2.4. Bootloader Installation

I installed GRUB for UEFI booting using:

grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --efi-directory=/boot --bootloader-id=ArchLinux

I generated the GRUB configuration and rebooted.

The first boot exposed a problem: the UEFI boot menu still contained entries from previous operating systems, including Kali Linux and Windows.

I inspected the UEFI boot entries and the files under /boot, then removed the obsolete entries.

After that, Arch Linux booted successfully.

### Result

I had a working minimal Arch Linux installation with:

  • A correctly mounted root filesystem.
  • An EFI System Partition.
  • GRUB configured for UEFI.
  • A regular user account.
  • Networking.
  • Basic system administration tools.

# 3. Building a Custom Graphical Environment

After completing the base installation, I decided to build my own desktop rather than install a full desktop environment.

I chose Hyprland because it provides a customizable Wayland compositor with dynamic window management, animations, workspaces, and extensive configuration options.

3.1. Components Installed

| Component | Role | Status | | --- | --- | --- | | Hyprland | Wayland compositor and window manager | Installed | | Kitty | Terminal emulator | Installed | | Dolphin | Graphical file manager | Installed | | Waybar | Customizable status bar | Installed | | Ly | Terminal-based display manager | Installed and enabled | | Wofi | Application launcher | Installed | | Mako | Notification daemon | Installed |

Some supporting components were also installed or tested during the setup process.

The exact package list should be reviewed before the next installation.

3.2. Understanding the Components

### Hyprland

Hyprland manages application windows and composites their graphical output into the Wayland session.

It is responsible for:

  • Window placement.
  • Workspaces.
  • Keyboard shortcuts.
  • Window focus.
  • Animations.
  • Window decorations.
  • Visual effects such as opacity and blur.

Hyprland is not a complete desktop environment by itself. Other applications and services provide functionality such as file management, notifications, application launching, and status information.

### Kitty

Kitty is a terminal emulator.

It provides a graphical interface in which I can run a shell such as Bash.

Kitty has its own configuration file, which can control its font, colors, cursor, padding, and background opacity.

### Dolphin

Dolphin is a graphical file manager from the KDE ecosystem.

It can run under Hyprland without requiring the entire KDE Plasma desktop.

It provides a graphical interface for navigating directories and managing files.

### Waybar

Waybar is a customizable status bar for Wayland compositors.

It can display:

  • Workspaces.
  • The current time and date.
  • Battery status.
  • Network information.
  • Audio volume.
  • System information.

Waybar uses its own configuration and CSS styling. Its appearance is separate from Hyprland's window decorations.

### Ly

Ly is a display manager that provides a text-based login interface.

I installed Ly and enabled its system service.

This allows me to log in and start my graphical session without manually launching Hyprland from a TTY each time.

### Wofi

Wofi provides an application launcher.

It can display applications discovered through desktop entries and can be assigned a keyboard shortcut in Hyprland.

### Mako

Mako is a notification daemon for Wayland.

It manages desktop notifications and supports customization of their appearance and behavior.

# 4. Hyprland Configuration: An Important Discovery

This was one of the most important lessons from my first installation.

4.1. Hyprland Uses Lua in My Installation

My installed version of Hyprland uses the newer Lua configuration system.

The standard configuration path is:

~/.config/hypr/hyprland.lua

This is different from the older configuration format:

~/.config/hypr/hyprland.conf

Hyprland 0.55 introduced Lua configuration, and the legacy configuration format is deprecated in favor of Lua.

The existence of an older .conf file does not mean that it is the active configuration.

In the newer system, if hyprland.lua exists, Hyprland loads it instead of the legacy .conf configuration when the compositor starts.

Therefore, the correct configuration format depends on the installed Hyprland version.

**My installation uses Lua, so I should use the Lua configuration API rather than copying instructions written for the legacy configuration format.**

Official reference: Hyprland configuration documentation.

4.2. My Configuration Troubleshooting Experience

Initially, I assumed Hyprland used hyprland.conf.

I attempted to create and modify a .conf file, but my changes did not affect the running desktop.

I investigated the problem using commands such as:

hyprctl reload

hyprctl configerrors

hyprctl getoption general:gaps_out

I also checked environment variables and attempted to inspect the running Hyprland process.

During this process, I discovered that the configuration file had been placed in the wrong directory.

I also discovered that the Lua file was the configuration actually controlling my desktop.

The Lua configuration contained a setting that kept gaps_out at 20, which explained why the active value remained unchanged when I modified the unrelated .conf file.

Once I corrected the configuration and its syntax, I was able to change settings and launch Waybar through the configuration.

### What I learned

A configuration file can exist without being the file that an application actually uses.

When troubleshooting configuration problems, I should verify:

1. Which configuration format my installed software version uses. 2. Where the active configuration is located. 3. Whether other files or modules override settings. 4. Whether the application reports configuration errors. 5. Whether the running application has loaded the expected values.

I should identify the active configuration before creating a new one.

4.3. Basic Lua Configuration Structure

Hyprland's Lua configuration uses the hl API.

For example, the configuration API has the following general structure:

hl.config({
    general = {
        gaps_in = 5,
        gaps_out = 20,
        border_size = 2,
    },
})

This example configures window spacing and border thickness.

The important point is that the settings are expressed as Lua tables passed to hl.config().

The legacy syntax:

general {
    gaps_in = 5
    gaps_out = 20
}

belongs to the older configuration format and should not be copied directly into a Lua file.

Lua also supports ordinary programming features such as variables, functions, conditionals, and modules.

This makes it possible to build a more sophisticated desktop configuration than a simple list of settings.

**Note:** The example above illustrates the configuration API. Before using additional functions or options, I should consult the documentation for my installed Hyprland version.

# 5. Starting Applications Automatically

Once I had a working Hyprland session, I wanted applications such as Waybar to launch automatically.

I configured the Lua file to start the necessary applications.

This allowed me to launch Hyprland and obtain a graphical desktop with Waybar running automatically.

I also verified that Dolphin and the other applications could run manually.

Important distinction: installation versus configuration

Installing a package does not necessarily make it run automatically.

For example:

  • Installing Waybar provides the executable.
  • Configuring Hyprland to launch Waybar starts it with the graphical session.
  • Configuring Waybar determines which modules it displays and how they look.

These are separate responsibilities.

The same principle applies to notifications, audio services, network applets, and other desktop components.

# 6. Understanding Ly

During my configuration work, I encountered an xinitrc file and wondered whether I should remove it.

The important distinction is between starting an X11 session manually and starting a Wayland session through a display manager.

6.1 What Is Ly?

Ly is a display manager that provides a login interface.

In my installation, I enabled its service so I could log in and start Hyprland directly.

My graphical login flow is approximately:

1. The computer boots. 2. The system starts the enabled Ly service. 3. Ly displays the login interface. 4. I authenticate and select or launch a session. 5. Hyprland starts. 6. Hyprland loads its Lua configuration. 7. The configured applications, including Waybar, start.

---

# 7. Customizing the Desktop

My initial objective was to create a functional desktop. After achieving that, I began exploring visual customization.

The next stage is to make the desktop feel personal rather than leaving it close to the default configuration.

7.1. Hyprland Appearance

Hyprland can control aspects of window appearance, including:

  • Window gaps.
  • Border thickness.
  • Rounded corners.
  • Window opacity.
  • Shadows.
  • Background blur.
  • Animations.
  • Window rules.
  • Workspace behavior.

These settings belong in the active Hyprland configuration and should be expressed using the Lua API supported by my version.

7.2. Kitty Appearance

Kitty can be customized independently.

Possible settings include:

  • Font and font size.
  • Background and foreground colors.
  • Cursor appearance.
  • Padding.
  • Background opacity.

Kitty's own background opacity is distinct from Hyprland's window opacity.

The two can be combined to create a translucent terminal appearance.

7.3. Waybar Appearance

Waybar uses CSS for visual styling.

I can customize:

  • Background colors.
  • Transparency.
  • Font and icon sizes.
  • Spacing.
  • Borders.
  • Module padding.
  • Layout.

Its configuration also determines which modules appear and in what order.

7.4. Other Components

Wofi and Mako can also be customized.

The objective is to create a consistent design across the entire desktop rather than independently styling each application without a common visual direction.

A coherent desktop should share a consistent color palette, typography, spacing, and visual language.

# 8. Dotfiles and Version Control

Dotfiles are configuration files used to customize applications and the user environment.

The term comes from the convention of naming hidden files and directories with a leading dot.

Many modern application configurations live under ~/.config/.

Examples include:

| Location | Purpose | | --- | --- | | ~/.config/hypr/ | Hyprland configuration | | ~/.config/waybar/ | Waybar configuration and CSS | | ~/.config/kitty/ | Kitty configuration | | ~/.config/wofi/ | Wofi configuration | | ~/.config/mako/ | Mako configuration | | ~/.bashrc | Bash shell configuration |

Not all applications use the same configuration format.

For example, Hyprland uses Lua in my installation, while Waybar uses its own configuration format and CSS.

Why maintain dotfiles?

A dotfiles repository allows me to:

  • Track configuration changes.
  • Revert mistakes.
  • Document my setup.
  • Reproduce my environment after reinstalling Arch.
  • Transfer my configuration to another computer.
  • Understand exactly which files control my desktop.

Git can track the files and their history.

A future repository might contain:

dotfiles/
├── hypr/
│   └── hyprland.lua
├── waybar/
│   ├── config
│   └── style.css
├── kitty/
│   └── kitty.conf
└── README.md

This is an illustrative organization, not a requirement.

I can use symbolic links or a dotfile manager to connect the repository to the locations where the applications expect their configurations.

I should avoid publishing secrets, tokens, credentials, or other sensitive information.
